baroque

/buh-ROHK/ - the stress falls on ROHK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Baroque means extravagantly ornate and elaborate — worked over layer upon layer, past all restraint.

The palace chapel is baroque to the last inch: not a hand's width of wall is left plain beneath the carved angels, the twisting marble garlands, and the gold.

Example

The organ recital closed with a baroque toccata whose every phrase blossomed into runs and trills; by the third minute the melody was somewhere underneath, carrying more ornament than it could bear.

Baroque works on both of the word's registers at once. Literally, the toccata belongs to the Baroque, the seventeenth-century style built on elaboration; critically, the performance is baroque because the ornament has swallowed what it was meant to decorate — the melody survives somewhere under the trills, but only just. When the elaboration takes over the thing itself, the word applies.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ornate: Ornate is rich decoration sitting on the surface of a thing — a carved frame, gilded covers, embroidered cuffs. Baroque goes further and deeper: the elaboration takes over the whole design, and the word stretches past objects to plans, rules, and prose.

extravagant: Extravagant measures excess of any kind, especially spending — an extravagant gift can be one enormous diamond on a plain band. Baroque names a particular shape of excess: layer upon layer of worked detail, curling over every surface.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plain: bare of decoration

austere: stripped to bare essentials by choice

Where it sits · how far the ornament takes over the design

fancy → baroque → rococo

fancy vs. baroque: Fancy is much milder than baroque — a ribbon here, a flourish there, decoration that still knows when to stop.

rococo vs. baroque: Rococo goes further than baroque: the ornament multiplies and turns playful until the structure underneath all but disappears.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — baroque: an irregular, lopsided pearl (French, from Portuguese barroco; the deeper origin is uncertain)

Put it together: Baroque came into English whole, from French baroque, in turn from Portuguese barroco — a jeweler's word for a pearl that grew lopsided instead of round. Critics borrowed the flaw as a sneer at the seventeenth century's swirling, over-elaborate art and architecture: irregular, extravagant, anything but a plain round pearl. The style outlived the insult, and the word kept both jobs — the name of a period, and a verdict on anything too elaborately worked.

Why there's no relative to spot: Portuguese barroco built nothing else in English — baroque arrived alone and stayed that way. Even rococo, the style-word most often spoken in the same breath, grows from a different root entirely (French rocaille, the pebble-and-shell garden work): neighbors in the showroom, not in the family tree.

Strength Check

Word Choice

critical when lowercase, neutral as the period name

Capitalized, Baroque names the seventeenth-century period — Bach's Baroque concertos are a classification, not a complaint. Lowercase, it is a verdict: extravagantly over-elaborated. And it is this unit's word for structure rather than surface — a contract, a bureaucracy, or an excuse can be baroque. Beside its unit-mates: florid describes overworked language and garish loud color, while baroque says the whole design has vanished under its own elaboration.
